title: Two Sum
problem: Return indices of two numbers whose sum equals target.
approach: Store previously seen values in a map and look up the complement.
constraints: At least two integers; exactly one pair exists. Return zero-based indices in either order; never reuse an index.
bruteForce: Compare every pair of distinct indices.
walkthrough: For [2,7,11,15], store 2 at index 0. At index 1 the complement is 2, so return [0,1]. Look up before inserting to avoid reusing the current index.
edgeCases: [3,3], target=6 → [0,1]; negative values; pair at the end.

title: Valid Anagram
problem: Check whether two lowercase English-letter strings have the same character counts.
approach: Count characters in a fixed-size array.
constraints: Inputs are non-null lowercase a-z strings. Return a boolean; unequal lengths cannot be anagrams.
bruteForce: For each source character, find and consume one matching unused target character.
walkthrough: Counting increments for s and decrements for t cancel exactly when all multiplicities match. Equal sets of characters alone are insufficient.
edgeCases: aab / abb → false; empty strings → true; different lengths.

title: Contains Duplicate
problem: Determine whether any value occurs more than once.
approach: Insert into a set; a failed insertion reveals a duplicate.
constraints: Input is a non-null integer array. Return true if any two different positions contain equal values.
bruteForce: Compare every index with every later index.
walkthrough: A HashSet contains precisely the previously visited values. In [1,2,3,1], the last insertion fails, revealing the duplicate.
edgeCases: [] → false; [1] → false; [1,1] → true.

title: Group Anagrams
problem: Group strings that contain the same letters with the same frequencies.
approach: Use a sorted character sequence as a canonical key.
constraints: Input is an array of lowercase a-z strings, including possible empty strings and duplicates. Return groups in any order; keep every occurrence.
bruteForce: Compare each word against the representative of every existing group using letter counts.
walkthrough: Sorting eat, tea and ate yields the same key aet. A canonical key avoids checking every existing group.
edgeCases: ["",""] → one group of two; duplicate words; singleton groups.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
problem: Return the k numbers with the highest occurrence counts.
approach: Count frequencies and maintain a min-heap of size k.
constraints: Nonempty integer array; 1 <= k <= distinct values. Assume the top-k set is unique; output order does not matter.
bruteForce: For each distinct value, scan the entire input to count it, then repeatedly pick the largest remaining count.
walkthrough: Counts are {1:3,2:2,3:1}. A heap capped at k removes the least frequent candidate, retaining 1 and 2 for k=2.
edgeCases: k=1; all values equal; k equals distinct count. Heap output is not necessarily sorted.

title: Product of Array Except Self
problem: Compute each index’s product of all other values without division.
approach: Multiply prefix products and then suffix products.
constraints: At least two integers; products of prefixes/suffixes fit int. Return one product per index, without division; zeros are allowed.
bruteForce: For each index multiply all other positions.
walkthrough: For [1,2,3,4], prefix values in output are [1,1,2,6]. A reverse suffix pass multiplies them by [24,12,4,1].
edgeCases: [0,2,3] → [6,0,0]; two zeros → all zero; negative values.

title: Valid Palindrome
problem: Ignore punctuation and case while testing whether a string reads the same backward.
example: "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama" → true
approach: Move two pointers inward, skipping non-alphanumeric characters.
constraints: Input is an ASCII string. Ignore non-alphanumeric characters and case. An empty normalized string is a palindrome.
bruteForce: Build a normalized string, reverse a copy, and compare.
walkthrough: Two pointers skip punctuation without allocating the normalized string. Each character is visited at most a constant number of times.
edgeCases: ".," → true; "race a car" → false; a single letter → true.

title: 3Sum
problem: Find unique triples of numbers summing to zero.
approach: Sort; fix one element and sweep the remaining pair.
constraints: Return distinct value triplets with sum zero, using three different indices. Output order does not matter. Assume abs(value) <= 100000.
bruteForce: Enumerate every index triple; sort each matching triple and deduplicate with a set.
bruteSpace: O(t) result storage for t unique triples
walkthrough: After sorting [-4,-1,-1,0,1,2], fixing -1 allows a two-pointer sweep to find (-1,-1,2) and (-1,0,1). Skip duplicate fixed values and matched endpoints.
edgeCases: [0,0,0,0] → [[0,0,0]]; fewer than three values; optimized code sorts input.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
problem: Maximize profit from one buy followed by one sell.
approach: Track the lowest price seen and best profit so far.
constraints: Non-null array of nonnegative daily prices. Choose at most one buy and a strictly later sell; return zero if no profit exists.
bruteForce: Try all buy/sell day pairs.
walkthrough: With [7,1,5,3,6,4], the minimum becomes 1 and selling at 6 yields 5. Keeping only the minimum eliminates repeated earlier-day scans.
edgeCases: Descending prices → 0; empty or singleton → 0; equal prices.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
problem: Find the maximum length of a substring with no repeated characters.
approach: Track last seen index and advance the left boundary.
constraints: Input is a non-null ASCII string. Return the length of a contiguous substring, not a subsequence, containing no duplicate characters.
bruteForce: Start at every index and grow a set until a character repeats.
walkthrough: In abcabcbb, the first window reaches abc. Seeing a again moves left past the previous a. Use max(left,last+1) so left never moves backward.
edgeCases: "abba" → 2; "" → 0; repeated spaces count as characters.

title: Valid Parentheses
problem: Determine whether bracket characters are correctly nested and closed.
approach: Push expected closing brackets and match them on encounter.
constraints: Input contains only (), [] and {}. Every closer must match the most recent unmatched opener; empty input is valid.
bruteForce: Repeatedly remove adjacent matching bracket pairs until no change occurs.
walkthrough: A stack stores expected closing characters. In ([]){}, ] must close [ before ) can close (. A nonempty stack at the end means missing closers.
edgeCases: "([)]" → false; "(" → false; "" → true.

title: Binary Search
problem: Find target in a sorted ascending array; return -1 if absent.
approach: Halve the remaining search range each step.
constraints: Input is a distinct-value ascending integer array. Return the zero-based target index or -1; empty input is allowed.
bruteForce: Scan every index until the target is found.
walkthrough: On [-1,0,3,5,9,12], midpoint 3 is too small for target 9. Discard indices 0..2, then locate 9 at index 4.
edgeCases: Empty array → -1; first/last index; absent target.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
problem: Find a target in a distinct-value sorted array rotated at a pivot.
approach: At each step identify the sorted half and discard the other.
constraints: Input was strictly ascending before rotation; all values are distinct. Return target index or -1 in O(log n) for the improved solution.
bruteForce: Ignore the rotation and scan every position.
walkthrough: For [4,5,6,7,0,1,2] and target 0, the left half through 7 is sorted but cannot contain 0. Search the right half. Distinct values make this choice unambiguous.
edgeCases: Unrotated input; singleton; absent target. Duplicates require a different algorithm and may cause linear behavior.

title: Maximum Subarray
problem: Find the largest sum of any nonempty contiguous subarray.
approach: Kadane’s algorithm chooses to extend or restart the current subarray.
constraints: Input has at least one integer. Return the largest sum of a nonempty contiguous subarray. Assume relevant sums fit int.
bruteForce: Enumerate every start/end pair and maintain a running sum for each start.
walkthrough: At each index Kadane keeps the best sum ending exactly there: extend the previous segment or start at the current value. [4,-1,2,1] sums to 6.
edgeCases: [-3,-1,-2] → -1, not zero; singleton; all zeros.

title: Climbing Stairs
problem: Count ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time.
approach: Each count equals the sum of the preceding two counts.
constraints: 1 <= n <= 45. Steps have size one or two; different orderings count separately. The answer fits int.
bruteForce: Recursively enumerate every possible next step without memoization.
walkthrough: Every path to step n ends with either a one-step move from n-1 or a two-step move from n-2. For n=4 the counts 2+3 give 5. Two variables replace repeated recursion.
edgeCases: n=1 → 1; n=2 → 2; n=45 fits int; brute force only for small n.

title: Coin Change
problem: Find the fewest coins needed for an amount, with unlimited coins of each denomination.
approach: Bottom-up DP stores minimum coins for every reachable amount.
constraints: Coins are positive integers with unlimited supply; amount >= 0. Return the minimum count or -1 if impossible. A zero amount needs zero coins.
bruteForce: Try every denomination recursively and choose the smallest successful result.
bruteTime: O(c^(A/m+1)) upper bound, c=coin count, A=amount, m=min coin
walkthrough: dp[a] stores the best count for amount a. For coins [1,2,5], dp[11] can use dp[6]+1=3. Initialize unreachable values above the maximum possible valid count.
edgeCases: [2], amount=3 → -1; amount=0 → 0; no zero/negative denominations; brute force only for small amounts.

title: Number of Islands
problem: Count connected groups of land cells in a 2D grid (4-directional adjacency).
approach: Flood-fill each unvisited land cell using an explicit stack.
constraints: Rectangular grid contains only 0 water and 1 land. Count components joined horizontally or vertically; diagonal contact does not join islands.
bruteForce: For every unassigned land cell repeatedly rescan the grid to expand its component until no adjacent land can be added.
walkthrough: Flood-fill marks land when pushing it, so each cell enters the stack once. The sample has one three-cell component and one isolated cell. The optimized solution mutates land to water; copy the grid if needed.
edgeCases: Empty grid → 0; all water → 0; diagonal land → separate islands; a long narrow island.

title: Merge Intervals
problem: Merge all overlapping closed intervals.
approach: Sort by start and merge when the next interval overlaps.
constraints: Each closed interval has start <= end. Touching endpoints overlap. Return disjoint merged intervals; empty input is allowed.
bruteForce: Repeatedly scan all interval pairs and merge any overlap until no pair overlaps.
walkthrough: Sort by start. After [1,3] merges with [2,6], current becomes [1,6]. [8,10] cannot overlap it, so emit current. Sorting guarantees later starts cannot reconnect a finished interval.
edgeCases: [[1,4],[4,5]] → [[1,5]]; nested intervals; optimized code sorts the input array.

title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
problem: Return the kth largest value (including duplicates).
approach: Keep a min-heap with at most k elements.
constraints: Nonempty array; 1 <= k <= n. Count duplicate values separately when ranking; return a value, not an index.
bruteForce: Repeatedly scan for the largest unused position k times.
walkthrough: A min-heap of size k retains the k largest values seen. Its root is the smallest of those retained values, which is exactly the kth largest overall.
edgeCases: [3,3,2], k=2 → 3; k=1; k=n; negative values.

title: House Robber
problem: Maximize money from nonadjacent houses.
approach: At each house, choose between skipping it or adding it to the best two houses back.
constraints: Non-null array of nonnegative house amounts. You may skip all houses; never select adjacent positions. Return maximum money; totals fit int.
bruteForce: At each index explore both skipping this house and taking it then skipping its neighbor.
walkthrough: For [2,7,9,3,1], running best values become 2,7,11,11,12. Taking a house uses the best two positions back; skipping uses the previous best.
